newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sentiment soft in Europe, range trade seen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sentiment soft in Europe, range trade seen.

text.p: The dollar started on a soft note in Europe, stalled by senior Japanese and German officials' comments which, though no longer actively driving the dollar down, were preventing the market from trying for higher levels.

Analysts saw the dollar stuck in a range against both the mark and yen today also because there were no major economic data due and because operators wanted to steer clear of roiling the market ahead of a G7 finance ministers' meeting next week.
"We have a background that makes for range trading. Certainly the dollar's momentum has been undermined," said Klaus Baader, senior currency ecoomist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Weighing the dollar down against the yen were remarks made overnight by Eisuke Sakakibara, the influential head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's international finance bureau.

Sakakibara, in an interview with Reuters, warned of the danger of assuming Japan would not raise interest rates within the next year, saying it would be natural for the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates when the strength of the economy was confirmed.
On currencies, he said intervention would be most effective when done when markets are not expecting it, adding that recent currency moves could not be justified by fundamentals.

"Sakakibara's comments seem more aggressive than before, it was like he was talking of intervention as something inevitable rather than potentially possible," said Joanne Collins, senior market strategist at Nomura International here.
The remarks pushed dollar/yen down to 125.65 yen in overnight trade. It had recovered to 126.01/08 by 0802 GMT, against 125.92/97 in late European trade on Wednesday.

"We're heading into the weekend, there's the G7 meeting next week and the (U.S.-Japan) bilateral meeting ahead of that, so I don't think the dollar's going to do much against the yen until then," Nomura's Collins said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto are scheduled to meet in Washington on April 25 to discuss various bilateral and international issues.

The dollar was also softer against the mark. Bulls were discouraged by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's comment on Thursday that the central bank was not interested in seeing the mark weaken further, although he also said the mark was reflecting economic fundamentals at its current levels.
Dollar/mark was at 1.7166/72 at 0809 GMT, near its overnight lows and down from 1.7220/26 in late European trade on Thursday.
"The Germans have given up their long-standing silence on exchange rates...and that's made a pretty significant impact on the market," DMG's Baader said.

"It's a lot less aggressive position than that of the Japanese... But the German position had been perceived as gladly accepting any depreciation of the mark, so in that sense it was an important statement, although it wasn't as strong as it might have been," Baader said.
The mark was up against other European currencies on Tietmeyer's comment, with the Norwegian crown struggling after hitting its lowest level against the mark since early January.
The British pound slipped against the mark, also due to Tietmeyer's comment, while it was firmer against the dollar on the back of dollar/yen's dip.
Sterling/mark was at 2.8015/20 against late Thursday's 2.8115/25, while cable was at $1.6318/30 against $1.6300/10.
